q: What does the monetary unit assumption say?
r: Business activity can be measured and recorded in money terms
Only items with a dollar value are recorded.
w: Every item must be recorded at its current market price each day
Money is the only thing that matters to a business owner
Currencies of different countries may be added together without conversion

q: A firm values a loyal workforce highly, but no dollar amount can be measured. How is it treated in the accounts?
r: It is not recorded as an asset
It cannot be reliably measured in money.
w: It is recorded as a large asset at any estimate
It is recorded as a liability

q: What is the time period assumption?
r: A business's life is divided into periods such as months or years for reporting
Statements cover specific periods.
w: A business must report only once at closing
All transactions are recorded on the same day each year
Each period must be exactly ten years

q: What is the historical cost principle also called?
r: The cost principle
Assets are recorded at purchase cost.

q: A business buys a building for $200,000 and its market value later reaches $260,000. What is the building's recorded value under the cost principle?
r: Assets stay at original cost.

q: What is owner's capital?
r: The owner's investment in the business plus earnings kept
It is the owner's claim on assets.
w: Money the business owes to banks
The cash held in a business bank account
The value of sales for the year

q: What is drawing (withdrawals)?
r: Assets the owner takes out of the business for personal use
It reduces owner's equity.

q: The owner withdraws $500 in cash. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
r: Assets and owner's equity both decrease by $500
The owner's claim falls with the cash.

q: What is a proprietorship's income statement item called 'cost of goods sold'?
r: The cost of merchandise that was sold
It is subtracted from sales to find gross profit.
w: The cost of rent for the year

q: What is merchandise inventory?
r: Goods a business holds for resale
It is a current asset.

q: Under the periodic inventory system, when is inventory updated in the records?
r: At the end of the period after a physical count
Records are adjusted after counting.

q: What is the perpetual inventory system?
r: A system that updates inventory records with each purchase and sale
It tracks stock continuously.
w: A system that updates inventory once a year
A system that records only cash sales

q: A store scans every sale and its stock records adjust instantly. Which system is this?
r: Perpetual inventory
Updates occur with each sale.

q: What does FIFO stand for?
r: First-in, first-out
Oldest costs are assumed sold first.

q: What does LIFO stand for?
r: Last-in, first-out
Newest costs are assumed sold first.

q: Purchases were 10 units at $5 then 10 units at $7. Ten units are sold. Under FIFO, what is cost of goods sold?
r: The first 10 units cost $5 each.

q: In a period of rising prices, which method usually reports the higher net income?
r: FIFO
Older, lower costs go to cost of goods sold.
w: It gives lower income in rising prices.

q: What is the purpose of the adjusted trial balance?
r: To check that debits equal credits after adjustments
It supports preparing statements.

q: Supplies on hand at year end are $300 and the supplies account shows $900. What adjustment amount is needed?
r: $600 to Supplies Expense
$900 minus $300 equals $600 used.
w: That is the amount on hand.

q: What is accrued interest receivable?
r: Interest earned but not yet received
It is recorded with an adjusting entry.

q: A $6,000 note at 8% was held for 3 months by year end with no interest received. What interest should be accrued?
What is the purpose of a post-closing trial balance?
r: To prove debits equal credits after closing entries are posted
Only permanent accounts appear.

q: What is a bad debt expense adjustment?
r: An entry that estimates uncollectible receivables
It matches the cost to the sales period.
w: An entry that records a cash sale
An entry that pays a supplier

q: Which accounts are closed at the end of the period?
r: Revenue, expense and drawing accounts
They are temporary.

q: What is a trade discount?
r: A reduction from a list price given to a buyer
It is not recorded as a separate account.

q: An item lists at $400 with a 25% trade discount. What is the invoice price?
r: $400 less $100 equals $300.

q: What is a purchases return?
r: Goods sent back to a supplier for credit
It reduces accounts payable.
w: Goods sent back by a customer

q: What is a debit memorandum?
r: A notice from a buyer to a seller that a payable is being reduced
It supports returns or allowances.
w: A bill sent by a seller

q: A credit memorandum issued by a seller to a customer does what to the customer's balance?
r: It reduces the amount owed
It supports returns or allowances.

q: What is days sales outstanding (DSO)?
r: The average number of days to collect receivables
Lower is generally better.
w: The number of days goods stay in stock
The number of days a supplier waits to be paid
The number of days in a fiscal year
That is the length of a year.

q: Receivables turnover is 12. About how many days does collection take using 360 days?
r: 30 days
360 divided by 12 equals 30.

q: What is the allowance method's balance sheet effect?
r: Receivables are shown net of expected losses
It reports a realistic collectible amount.
w: Receivables are shown at double their value
Receivables are shown only in cash

q: What is retained earnings?
r: Accumulated profits kept in the business instead of paid out
It appears in a corporation's equity.

q: A corporation starts with $50,000 retained earnings, earns $20,000 and pays $5,000 in dividends. What is the ending balance?
What is a classified balance sheet?
r: A balance sheet that groups items into categories such as current and long-term
It helps readers analyze position.
w: A balance sheet that is kept secret
A balance sheet printed in a special font
A balance sheet with only assets

q: What are intangible assets?
r: Assets without physical form, such as patents and trademarks
They have value but cannot be touched.
w: Assets you can touch, such as machinery

q: Which is an intangible asset?
r: A patent
It has value but no physical form.

q: What is goodwill?
r: The extra amount paid for a business above the value of its identifiable assets
It reflects reputation and customer base.
w: The cash left after paying all bills
A fee paid to a bank

q: What is earnings per share?
r: Net income divided by the number of shares outstanding
It shows profit per share.
w: That is a ratio of position.

q: A company earns $600,000 and has 200,000 shares outstanding. What is its EPS?
r: $600,000 divided by 200,000 equals $3.

q: What does return on assets (ROA) measure?
r: How efficiently a company uses its assets to earn profit
Net income divided by total assets.
w: How much cash a company has
How much debt a company owes

q: Net income is $90,000 and total assets are $900,000. What is ROA?
r: $90,000 divided by $900,000 equals 0.10.

q: What is revenue recognition's five-step idea based on?
r: Recording revenue when control of goods or services passes to the customer
Timing follows delivery.
w: Recording revenue when the order is first discussed
Recording revenue when the check is printed
Recording revenue only at year end

q: What is a material misstatement?
r: An error large enough to change a reader's decisions
Auditors look for them.
w: A tiny typo with no effect
A correct entry in the ledger

q: A $5 rounding error in a $10 million statement is most likely:
r: Immaterial
It would not change decisions.

q: What is an internal audit?
r: A review by company staff of controls and records
It supports management.
w: A review by the tax agency only

q: What does separation of duties help prevent?
r: Fraud and errors
No one controls a whole process.

q: Which situation violates separation of duties?
r: One person orders, receives and pays for supplies
One person controls the whole cycle.
w: One person orders and another pays

q: What is the Fair Credit Reporting Act's concern?
r: Accuracy and privacy of consumer credit information
Consumers can dispute errors.

q: What is an EIN?
r: A federal Employer Identification Number issued to a business
It is used for payroll and tax filings.

q: Which business is most likely to need an EIN?
r: One that hires employees
Employers use it for payroll.
w: It usually does not need one.
A person washing their own car

q: What is Form 941 used for?
r: Employers reporting quarterly payroll taxes
It reports withheld income and FICA taxes.

q: What is a W-9 form?
r: A form a contractor gives a business with their taxpayer information
The business uses it to prepare a 1099.
w: A form employees use to set withholding
A form for filing a return

q: A business pays a freelancer $4,000 in a year. Which form does it generally send the freelancer?
r: Form 1099-NEC
It reports nonemployee compensation.

q: What is an estimated tax payment?
r: A quarterly payment of expected income tax by people without withholding
It avoids a large year-end bill.
w: A guess about next year's tax law
A refund sent by the government

q: What is a sales tax permit?
r: Government permission for a seller to collect sales tax
Sellers must remit the tax collected.

q: What is electronic invoicing?
r: Sending and receiving invoices digitally
It speeds up billing and payment.

q: Which is a benefit of automated invoicing?
r: Fewer manual errors and faster collection
Systems send and track invoices.

q: What is a digital signature?
r: An electronic way to verify who signed a document
It supports secure approvals.
w: A scanned drawing of a pet
A printed name on a letter

q: What is data analytics software used for in accounting?
r: Finding patterns, trends and unusual items in financial data
It supports decisions and audits.

q: An auditor uses software to scan all transactions for duplicate payments. What is this?
r: Data analytics for fraud detection
It tests entire data sets.
w: Manual sampling of a few items

q: What does a credit analyst do?
r: Assesses whether people or businesses can repay loans
They review financial information.

q: What is the CPA exam known for?
r: Testing accounting knowledge as part of becoming licensed
Education and experience rules also apply.

q: A student likes analyzing budgets and advising managers on spending. Which role fits best?
r: Management accountant or budget analyst
These roles support internal decisions.
